title: Lunceford's ninety one-nighters and being refused food
summary: The band played endless one-nighters, and Will Smith, who looks white, bought sandwiches for the band where they were not served.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh, Lunceford, we did a lot of good -- we did so many one-nighters though, Whew. You know, we did more one-nighters than I think than anybody. Yeah, Lunceford's band. We -- sometimes we'd do 90 or more in a row, you know. Just -- you'd be so dead when you left, so tired, and so glad to get a day off or something like that because it was rough, you know. You couldn't get decent food, and traveling.
I remember one night we were going somewhere down Florida. And we got through a job and we got -- we couldn't go nowhere to eat. So, Will X Smith, he looks white anyway.

So, we sent him in a place. Sure enough, he got a lot of sandwiches for us, about $30.00 worth of sandwiches. But we couldn't go into the place. So, you know, he went in and got it. Things were that bad back there then. You know, New York was even bad. You know the story --
Oh, yeah. At one time. I mean not that bad but, you know, when Billy ie Holiday was singing with Artie Shaw they wanted her to come in the back door, you know.
Yeah, right. But that was mixing (inaudible).
But when -- so long as people kept separate, there was a place to get something to eat, wasn't there?
You could eat. New York wasn't that bad but it had its bad points. It wasn't as bad as that South was down there. Things were kind of rugged, you know.
Willie had a sort of strange dual-existance.
He could go in and get food --

Yeah, but he had a problem down South when he played down South because once a policeman once told him come off that bandstand. He said, you can't be playing with them. You come off that stand. But he had to carry his birth certificate around with him. That's the only way we could -- he could get to play with us.
